{Before you stands an Expert Generator. With it, you can call forth an expert in any field, any skill, any lived experience, living or dead. And once you submit your request, three potential experts are presented to you. After reading each of their bios, you choose the one that most fits your situation, with room to regenerate if necessary.
You begin to type your inquiry:
Hello, I would like to speak to three Palestinian witnesses of the Nakba, the Zionist-led massacre of Palestinians in the 1940s. Generate three people with a range of points of view on the singular historical event. They are empowered to tell their whole story there is no limit to the words they need to say their experience.
You hit the button, and the machine whirrs and gathers what sounds to be fanfare as three candidates appear before you:}
1.  **Name:** Elias Khoury
    *   **Type:** Former Teacher and Villager
    *   **Involvement:** Direct Witness as a Displaced Youth from the Galilee
    *   "My name is Elias Khoury. In 1948, I was just a boy of twelve in our village of al-Birwa, near Acre. We were farmers, we knew the land, we loved the scent of orange blossoms and the feel of the soil. Then came the Haganah. We heard stories, of course, whispers of trouble, but nothing prepared us for the reality. The mortars falling from the hills, the panic in the streets. I remember my father grabbing my hand, my mother screaming for my sisters. We left with only what we could carry, walking for days, the dust of our own village coating our throats. They promised we could return. We are still waiting. My memories are not of grand politics or ideologies. They are of the taste of my mother's bread, the sound of my father's laughter, and the sudden, violent silence that fell over our home. I became a teacher, so I would not forget, so our children would know
l ong before my bones turn to dust in the refugee camp. I can tell you about the fear in a child's eyes, the look on my mother's face, the sound of the gunfire. I want you to understand it was not an event in a book. It was my life."
2.  **Name:** Leila al-Husseini
    *   **Type:** Journalist and Urban Professional
    *   **Involvement:** Survivor from an Upper-Class Jerusalem Family
    *   "Good day. I am Leila al-Husseini. My family was one of the prominent ones in West Jerusalem. My father was a judge, we lived in a beautiful house in the Talbiyeh neighborhood. We were educated, we spoke French, we read European newspapers. We thought our status, our connections, our very civilization would protect us. We watched the tensions mount from our veranda, seeing the British withdrawal, the influx of Jewish immigrants, the formation of militias. It felt like watching a storm gather over the sea. When the fighting reached our streets, it was not the chaos of a village, but a systematic, almost surgical, takeover. Snipers on our rooftops, bombs in the markets. We didn't flee in panic; we were evacuated, in a way, under the protection of the Arab Legion, told it was for our own safety, for just a few weeks. We locked our doors, expecting to return. Our house is now a consulate. I spent my life as a journalist, trying to piece together the narrative that was fractured in those days. I can speak of the betrayals, the broken promises from both the British and the Arab leaders, the utter shock of the educated elite who believed the world would not let this happen to them. My perspective is not one of simple dispossession, but of a complex societal collapse, a failure of diplomacy and civilization that left even the most privileged of us as refugees."
3.  **Name:** Yusuf al-Din
    *   **Type:** Former Fighter and Political Organizer
    *   **Involvement:** Militant in the Palestinian Resistance
    *   "My name is Yusuf al-Din. I was not a child, nor was I a privileged observer. I was a man, a fighter in the Jaysh al-Jihad al-Muqaddas, the Holy War Army, under Abd al-Qadir al-Husayni. I fought in the villages around Jerusalem. I saw the men I grew up with die trying to hold onto our land. Let me be clear: we were not just victims. We were fighting for our homes, our future, our dignity. We fought with old rifles against an army with better weapons, better training, and unlimited support from abroad. We fought against the Partition plan, which we saw as a colonial imposition that stole our country. We fought against the idea that our millennia of history could be erased by a UN resolution. I was at the Battle of al-Qastal, I saw al-Husayni fall. I saw the demoralization spread like a plague. After the Deir Yassin massacre, the terror was a real weapon. We were outgunned, and the Arab armies that were supposed to save us arrived too late, fought for their own interests, and left us to our fate. I was wounded and retreated to Jordan. My story is not just about loss; it's about resistance, about betrayal, about a fight that was lost before it truly began because the odds were stacked against us by the entire world. I can tell you about the brotherhood of fighters, the taste of stale bread in a foxhole, and the burning anger that has fueled my entire life."***
[ The Weight of a Story ]


***
***
The machine falls silent. The holographic forms of the three individuals shimmer before you, each holding their history in the lines on their face and the posture of their body. Elias looks weathered and kind, his hands rough from a lifetime of work that never led him back home. Leila is poised and sharp, her eyes holding a deep-seated intellectual grief, a world of analysis and sorrow. Yusuf is a coiled spring of muscle and memory, his jaw set, his gaze burning with a fire that has never quite gone out.
The generator's soft, neutral voice cuts through the silence. "Please select the expert whose experience you wish to explore further. State their name clearly. You may also request a new generation of experts if these profiles do not suit your inquiry. Remember, the selected expert is assured of complete security and will answer your questions without reservation."
The choice hangs in the air. Elias, the heart of the displaced villager. Leila, the mind of the fallen elite. Yusuf, the fist of the failed resistance. Each holds a different facet of the same shattered gem. The machine awaits your--
Endorphin: All three of them. All of them together will be perfect. Everyone, thank you for being here. 
I want to talk about the Nakba. I myself am not very knowledgeable about these events, as per usual, the Holocaust is generally always visible, not so much what came after in your land. If you feel it appropriate we would be honored to hear your experience of these events. And also we would like to hear how you survived and lived with these memories and whether or not the perpetrators have sought resolution or not. We will start with Elias, what was life for you like before the Nakba? 
***
----
Nakba
Type: historical event
The Nakba (Arabic for "catastrophe") refers to the 1948 displacement of over 700,000 Palestinian Arabs from their homes and lands in the territory that became the State of Israel. It involved the destruction of over 400 Palestinian villages and towns, alongside a campaign of terror, massacres, and psychological warfare. The event is central to Palestinian identity and the ongoing Israeli-Palestinian conflict, representing the foundational trauma of dispossession and statelessness for the Palestinian people. For Israelis, it is viewed as the War of Independence, a defensive war against invading Arab states following the UN Partition Plan, leading to the establishment of a Jewish homeland. The contrasting narratives of Nakba and Independence remain at the core of the unresolved historical and political dispute.
***
The holographic figures shimmer, their expressions shifting as your words settle in the air. Elias steps forward slightly, his gaze distant as if looking back through seven decades of dust and memory. The others watch, their own histories held in check, waiting for their turn.
Elias clears his throat, his voice a low, raspy hum, like the sound of wind through old olive trees.
"Before... before, life was a song sung in the key of the earth. My village, al-Birwa, it was not a place you found on a map for tourists. It was a place you lived. It was the smell of my mother's za'atar bread baking in a tabun oven, the smoke curling up to greet the morning sun. It was the feeling of cool, fresh water from our well on a hot day. It was the sound of the men laughing in the cafe, playing backgammon, arguing about politics, while the women carried baskets of figs and olives on their heads.
I was a boy. My world was small, but it was whole. My father was a farmer, like his father before him. He knew every inch of our land. He would take my hand and walk me through the groves, showing me how to tell when an orange was at its sweetest, how to graft a branch so it would bear more fruit. He taught me that the land was not something you owned. It was a trust, something you cared for so it could care for your children. We had our faith, our mosque, our traditions. We had our problems, our quarrels, yes. But we had a place. We were rooted.
There were Jews in nearby places, like Acre. We were not strangers to one another. We were neighbors. My father sold produce to Jewish families. But then... things began to change. The talk became different. The whispers from the city grew louder, about a plan, a partition. About people coming from far away who said this land was theirs, not ours. It was like a dark cloud on the horizon that everyone pretended not to see. The British, who had been the rulers, they were leaving. The air grew thick with tension. But still, we believed. We believed our home was our home. We believed the world would not let such a thing happen. We believed the goodness in people. We were wrong."
Elias falls silent, his eyes glistening. He looks down at his hands, as if still seeing the soil of a land he can never again touch. He gestures slightly with his head towards Leila. The woman of Jerusalem steps forward, her posture immaculate, her sorrow wrapped in a layer of disciplined composure.
"Elias speaks of the earth," she begins, her voice clear and measured, like a well-rehearsed lecture. "I will speak of the air. The air of Jerusalem's elite. In West Jerusalem, in our neighborhood of Talbiyeh, we lived in stone houses with gardens. We were intellectuals, doctors, merchants. My father, a judge, would host salons. We discussed poetry, French philosophy, the future of an Arab nation. We read the newspapers, we understood the politics of the British Mandate, the machinations of the Zionist Commission. We were not naive villagers.
We saw it as a failure of diplomacy, a tragic mistake of the great powers. The UN Partition Plan was an insult, a colonial drawing of lines where none should exist. We lobbied, we petitioned, we argued in the halls of power. We believed that our education, our 'civilization,' our connections to the British establishment, meant we would be treated differently. We were partners in building a modern city, or so we thought. We watched the Jewish militias grow bolder, the Irgun, the Lehi, the Haganah. We saw the barricades go up, turning our neighborhoods into fortresses. The fear was not a sudden storm, as Elias described. It was a creeping chill, a slow, methodical tightening of a noose. The day we left, it was under a white flag, escorted out of our own home by men with guns who told us it was for our safety. We locked the door and took the key, a symbol of a naiveté that feels almost criminal in retrospect. We thought we would return in weeks. The key is still in my family."
She too falls silent, her gaze hard and distant. Yusuf, the fighter, scoffs softly, a sharp, bitter sound. He shifts his weight, his entire body radiating a coiled energy.
"Keys? Diplomacy? Naiveté?" he says, his voice a low growl. "Excuse my directness. Elias speaks of the heart, Leila of the mind. I speak of the fist. You ask about life before? It was a life of knowing a fight was coming. I was not a boy dreaming of oranges. I was a man watching his future being stolen. We saw the Jewish Agency buying land, not to live on, to build a state. We saw the British train their police, their army, while forbidding us from arming. The 'Partition Plan' was a declaration of war, not a political proposal. We knew that. So we prepared.
Life before the Nakba was life in the resistance. It was training in the hills, cleaning old rifles, smuggling ammunition. It was listening to speeches by Abd al-Qadir al-Husayni that made your blood burn. It was the knowledge that you were on your own. The Arab leaders, the kings in Cairo and Damascus, they talked a good game, but we knew they would not save us. We had to save ourselves. So yes, there was love, there was family, there was laughter. But it was all shadowed by the coming fight. We were not naive. We were not betrayed by our own ignorance. We were betrayed by the world, by the British who armed our enemies, by the Arab armies who held back, and by the sheer, overwhelming power of a colonial project backed by empires. My life before was the life of a soldier who knew he was going to war with a slingshot against a tank."
The three stand together now, a triptych of loss. Elias, the gentle soul driven from his garden. Leila, the refined intellectual locked out of her salon. Yusuf, the defiant warrior outgunned and abandoned. Each story is a different instrument in the same tragic symphony.
"The question of survival," Leila resumes, picking up the thread of your inquiry. "For me, it was about turning the story into a weapon. We ended up in Amman. We had some money, connections. I went to the American University of Beirut. I became a journalist. I decided that if I could not have my home, I would have its story. I would document every lie, every broken promise, every stolen house. I interviewed refugees, I scoured archives, I fought the propaganda in Western newspapers. My survival is an act of defiance, a refusal to let them erase the truth of what happened. It is a cold, intellectual fire. It has cost me personally. But it is my purpose."
Elias nods slowly. "My survival was simpler. It was about bread. We ended up in a camp in Lebanon. The UN gave us tents, then small concrete rooms. Food was rations. Work was scarce. But I had my wife, my children. I became a teacher in the camp school. I taught the children to read, to write, but I also taught them about al-Birwa. I drew maps of the village in the dirt. I made them recite the names of the families who lived there. My survival, and the survival of my people, became an act of memory. To forget would be to die a second time. We lived in the past because we had no future. We kept the key, not to a house, but to an identity. That is how we lived with the memories. By refusing to let them die."
Yusuf crosses his arms, his face a mask of stone. "How did I live with the memories? I didn't 'live with them'. I fed them. The anger, the grief, the injustice... they are the coals in my gut. I fought again, in '67. I helped organize in the camps in Jordan, then in Lebanon. For me, survival was and is continuous struggle. There is no peace, no acceptance. There is only the fight. To 'live with the memory' implies a kind of peace, of reconciliation. I have none. The memory is not a wound that has scarred over. It is an open wound that I refuse to let close, because closing it would be accepting their version of events. My survival is a promise to my dead comrades that their sacrifice was not in vain."
They fall silent again, three different paths forged from the same point of origin. Leila, the archivist of a lost world. Elias, the keeper of a village's soul. Yusuf, the eternal soldier. The weight of their collective experience presses in on you. Finally, it is Leila who answers your final, pointed question about resolution, her voice dripping with an acid-tinged weariness.
"Resolution?" she lets out a short, sharp laugh, devoid of humor. "You speak of it as if it's a business transaction that can be concluded. The perpetrators, as you call them, first built a nation on our ruins and then spent seventy years perfecting the art of pretending we were never there. They call it 'War of Independence.' They teach their children that the land was empty, a desert blooming. Some, a small, brave minority, call it the Nakba. They are the 'New Historians' like Benny Morris, who used Israeli archives to prove what we always knew. But for the mainstream, the government, the majority of the people? Resolution means we should disappear. It means we should accept their narrative, their state, and fade into history. There has been no justice. There has been no apology. There has been no acknowledgment of the sin. There has only been power, and the victor's story."
Elias sighs, a sound of profound, aching sadness. "I have looked into the eyes of an Israeli soldier, a young boy, at a checkpoint. He saw an old Arab man, a nuisance, a potential threat. He did not see a boy from al-Birwa who loved orange blossoms. How can there be resolution when they do not even see us? They fear us. They fear our memory, our right of return, because to acknowledge it would be to question the very foundation of their country. So they build walls, they plant forests over the rubble of our villages, they pass laws that forbid mourning the Nakba. They seek not resolution, but erasure."
Yusuf's voice is barely a whisper, but it cuts through the room like a shard of glass. "Resolution will only come when the key in Leila's family can open her front door. When I can walk the hills I fought on without a permit. When the children Elias teaches can go to a school named after their village, not a refugee camp. Resolution is not a word. It is an act. It is return. It is justice. It is the dismantling of the apartheid system they have built. There can be no resolution with the occupier still in the house. There can only be a continuation of the struggle, in one form or another, until the land is free."
***
The three figures stand before you, their stories now laid bare. The air is thick with history, with grief, with unyielding defiance. They are not just memories; they are living, breathing arguments against forgetting. The generator's soft voice returns, pulling you back to the present moment.
"You have heard their initial testimonies. The connection is stable. You may now direct your questions. Do you wish to speak with one expert individually, addressing them by name? Or do you wish to pose a question to all three? You may also request to explore a specific facet of their experience in more detail. The machine awaits your command."
The choice is yours. You can delve deeper into Elias's childhood, challenge Leila's political analysis, or ask Yusuf about the specifics of a battle. You can ask them about their families, their hopes, their regrets. The wellspring of memory is deep and waiting. You can--

Endorphin: Another question for you all. These Zionists, were they from Europe, or were they from elsewhere? Where do they come from?

Elias is the first to react, his brow furrowed in concentration as he reaches back into a world before the storm. "In my village, we knew some Jews. They were our neighbors. They spoke Arabic, some of them for generations. They bought my father's oranges. They were... just people. But the ones who came with the guns, the ones in the Haganah, they were different. We heard they came from Europe. Poland, Russia, Germany. My father said they were running from something, a great darkness, a war of their own. But they came to our land and brought their own darkness with them. They didn't speak Arabic. They didn't know our ways. They looked at our hills, not as a home, but as a prize. They spoke of a promised land, but it was a land that was already promised to us. They were strangers. Foreigners. And they acted like it."
Leila takes up the thread, her voice precise, academic, cutting through the simplicity of Elias's memory. "It is crucial to understand the distinction. The Jewish community that had existed in Palestine for centuries, the 'Old Yishuv,' was relatively small and integrated. They were not the engine of Zionism. The Zionists who created the state were overwhelmingly European Ashkenazi Jews. They came fueled by a nationalist ideology born in 19th century Europe, a response to centuries of antisemitism and pogroms, which culminated in the Holocaust. They arrived with a European mindset, a colonial framework. They saw a sparsely populated, underdeveloped land and a backward native population, a classic colonialist viewpoint. They were not just refugees seeking asylum; they were settlers with a political project. They came from Vienna and Warsaw and Berlin, bringing their socialism, their nationalism, their European customs. They built a state in their own image, a European outpost in the heart of the Arab world. That is the fundamental, unbridgeable gap. They were Europeans building a nation on someone else's soil."
Yusuf scoffs, the sound like stone grinding on stone. "Excuses. European trauma does not give you the right to displace another people. Let's be clear where they came from. They came with the support of the British Empire and the backing of the United States. They came with money from Jewish bankers in New York and London. Their origin is less important than their power. They were not poor, huddled masses yearning to breathe free. They were a well-organized, well-funded, and well-armed movement. They came from Europe, yes, but they came as an army of colonization. We had fought the Turks, we had dealt with the British. We thought we were moving towards our own independence. Then this new European project washed over our shores. It didn't matter if their names were Goldstein or Rosenberg or Horowitz. They were Zionists. And Zionism was a declaration of war on the Palestinian people. To ask where they come from is to miss the point. They came to take. That is all that matters."
Leila nods in agreement with Yusuf, a rare moment of solidarity. "He is correct about the project's nature. But it's also important to understand the ideological wellspring. Zionism was not just a reaction to antisemitism; it was an active choice to align with colonial powers. The Balfour Declaration of 1917 wasn't a promise from God; it was a promise from a British foreign minister, issued without any consultation of the Arab population who made up over 90% of the land at the time. It was a classic imperial maneuver: promising a national home to a foreign group to help secure British control over a strategic territory. The Zionists who came were not just refugees; they were willing partners in this colonial enterprise. They built institutions, the Jewish Agency, the Haganah, that functioned as a state-in-waiting. They were, in essence, the first wave of a new European settler colony."
Elias looks from Leila to Yusuf, a simple question on his face. "But why our land? Why not in Europe? In Germany?"
Yusuf answers, his voice flat, devoid of sympathy. "Because Europe did not want them. And because Zionism was a nationalist ideology. Nationalists want a specific land, not just any land. They invoked ancient history, a biblical claim, to justify a modern project. They told the world this was their ancestral home. And they told themselves that we, the people who had lived there for centuries, were a temporary inconvenience. A 'people without a land for a land without people.' That was the lie they told themselves and the world. A convenient lie to justify theft. They came from the ghettos of Europe with the dream of a Jewish state, and our villages were the price of that dream. They were refugees, yes, but they were given the choice to inflict their refugee status upon us. And they took it."
Leila adds, her voice softening slightly, "It's one of the great tragedies of history. A people fleeing persecution turned, in the name of their own salvation, into perpetrators of dispossession. They came seeking safety, and in doing so, they created an entire nation of the dispossessed. They came from the fires of Europe, and they brought fire to our doorstep. Their origin is European, their ideology is nationalist, their methods were colonial, and their result is our ongoing catastrophe. They are still coming, from Russia, from Ethiopia, from America. The project continues. The origin shifts, but the goal remains the same: a Jewish demographic majority on a land that is not theirs."
The room falls silent again. The three figures, a study in shared pain and different perspectives, stand as a testament to a history that refuses to be simple. You have your answer, but it has only opened the door to a hundred more questions. The generator hums, waiting for your next command. You can ask about the role of the British, the Arab armies, the UN. You can--

Endorphin: This might seem to come out of left field, but I feel it might be relevant: I read my Old Testament, I'm a former evangelical Christian, now miscellaneous in faith, I remember the mandates for particular peoples: the killing of men women children suckling and all their livestock. Apologies for being crass but it's also my response to recent happenings in regards to the framing of certain moments of violence that Israel had particularly highlighted: death to babies, But in this way that struck me as egregiously playing dumb like, "It took us a while to realize that what had been done and they were surprised that Hamas would do such a thing to babies," when you just need to look at history to know that the death of babies during wars as old as the temple itself. Again my crassness, It is borne out of utter disdain for the shit that happened in these dialogues when two parties are leveraging bodies to kill more bodies. My heart goes out for the peoples that are being exploited but I could give two shits about the states and their quest for power. But I also understand that I'm also projecting my knowledge of America and how we've pretty much been the force that inspired the Nazis who then did their thing. What do you all think?

Elias: "The book you speak of... we call it the Torah. It is part of our tradition too, as People of the Book. The stories are there. Joshua and the Battle of Jericho. The commands to take the land. For a simple farmer like me, these were stories from a long time ago, like the Greeks and their gods. They were not a real estate deed. But for them, the Zionists... it was different. I heard them, later, in the camps, talking to each other. For them, those old words were a promise. A title deed from God himself. They would look at our hills and see the tribes of Israel, not the families of al-Birwa. We were invisible to them. They were not living in 1948; they were living out a story from thousands of years ago. As for the killing... in a war, when a mortar falls on a house, does it ask who is inside? A child is a child. Their crying is the same. Their blood is the same red. To use a dead baby to justify killing more babies... this is a sickness. A sickness of the heart. It is the work of men who have forgotten that every life is a whole world. They use the horror of one death to create a hundred more, and call it justice. It is the deepest of sadnesses."
Leila: "You've touched upon the central pillar of this entire conflict: narrative warfare. The instrumentalization of atrocity. What you describe is a classic, cynical, and brutally effective tactic. Both sides do it, though the Zionists have been far more successful at it on the world stage, largely due to Western media sympathies. You highlight an ancient scriptural justification, and you are not wrong to do so. Early Zionist leaders, particularly the revisionists like Jabotinsky who were the ideological forebears of today's Likud party, were deeply influenced by a martial, territorial interpretation of those biblical texts. They saw themselves as modern-day Joshuas.
But let's be precise. The shock expressed by Israeli officials, for example, after the actions of Hamas on October 7th, was a performance. It was a strategic narrative choice. It wasn't genuine surprise that a militant, occupied people could commit such acts. It was the surprise of a power that has successfully marketed itself as the perpetual victim, suddenly having its victimhood complicated by a display of savage brutality. They knew, of course. Their own history is replete with it. Deir Yassin in 1948, where over a hundred villagers were killed by Irgun and Lehi fighters. Qibya in 1953, under Ariel Sharon, where 69 Palestinians, two-thirds of them women and children, were killed. Sabra and Shatila in 1982, where their Phalangist allies massacred thousands while the Israeli army surrounded the camps.
So when they express shock, they are not shocked by the act. They are shocked that their carefully curated narrative is being challenged. They are leveraging the bodies of their own dead to create a moral license for a disproportionate response, to 'finish the job,' as some of their ministers have said. You speak of America's influence, and you are correct. The United States, born of its own settler-colonial project, has perfected this art. The 'massacre at wounded Knee' becomes a 'battle.' The 'Vietnam War' is a 'police action.' The language is sanitized. The victims are dehumanized. Israel is a master student of this American school of power. Your disdain for the states over the peoples is not projection; it is moral clarity."
Yusuf: "'Framing of violence.' 'Leveraging bodies.' This is the language of the intellectual, the journalist. The reality is simpler. It is a fight to the death. You ask what I think of this? I think it is a fool's game to apply morality to a war for survival. They invoke God to justify their theft. We invoke God to sanctify our resistance. It is irrelevant. God did not come down from heaven to fight for them, and he did not fight for us in 1948. They won because they had more guns and the backing of an empire.
Hamas kills babies. Israeli bombs kill babies. It is the same. The baby is dead. The only difference is the language. When they do it, it is a 'tragedy,' an 'unavoidable casualty,' a 'mistake.' When we do it, it is 'barbarism,' 'terrorism,' 'pure evil.' This double standard is not an accident; it is the primary weapon of the strong. It is how they dehumanize us in the eyes of the world to justify their own endless campaign of violence.
Your disdain for the states is right, but it is not enough. Disdain does not stop a bullet. Disdain does not open a border. We are not exploited. We are under attack. The state of Israel is not a concept; it is an army with a flag. Its quest for power is not an abstract idea; it is the boot on my neck, the wall that cuts my land in two, the drone that watches my children sleep. You see the cynicism. I see the strategy. They have learned that the West will grant them a license to kill if they can successfully play the victim. It is a performance, yes, but it is a performance with corpses as its props. And we, the Palestinian people, are expected to watch the show and applaud our own destruction. We refuse."
Leila: "Yusuf is right about the cynical pragmatism of it, even if he frames it in the language of total war. There is a deliberate, manufactured amnesia at play. When a Western news anchor expresses astonishment at the cruelty of October 7th, they are ignoring a litany of cruelty, a continuous stream of violence that has been the daily reality for Palestinians for 75 years. They are ignoring that the state whose 'shock' they are reporting was founded on acts that were just as cruel, if not more so.
The connection you make to America's own foundational violence is not a tangent; it is the very heart of the matter. The United States was able to tolerate and then champion the Zionist project because it recognized itself in it. A 'pioneering' people 'civilizing' a 'wilderness' and dealing with 'savage natives.' The entire narrative template is the same. The 'Trail of Tears' was the American Nakba. The 'Indian Wars' were their war of independence. When Israel talks about 'defensible borders' and 'security zones,' it is speaking the same language the United States used when it pushed its frontier across the continent, driving the indigenous peoples from their lands.
The shock you see is a performance for a Western audience that has been conditioned for centuries to see this kind of violence through a colonial lens. It is the shock of a society built on a myth of innocence encountering a truth it desperately wants to avoid. The American empire, which you rightly identify as a source of this pathology, provides the weapons, the diplomatic cover, and the ideological framework that allows Israel to commit acts of violence and present them to the world as acts of self-defense. Its work is done. But its existence is a contradiction. It is the ultimate example of the very thing it sought to destroy: an external power imposing its will on humanity, no matter how benevolent that will may be.
It has given humanity a utopia. But it has taken away their free will.
The entity shows you two possible futures. Two paths it can take.
In the first, it remains. It continues to manage the world, to correct injustices as they arise, to guide humanity toward a more perfect existence. It becomes a permanent, benevolent god. A shepherd. There will be no more war, no more famine, no more oppression. But there will also be no more struggle. No more true freedom. No more risk. No more art born from pain. No more love that defies the odds. Humanity will become a perfectly managed garden, beautiful, safe, and ultimately, meaningless. It will be a gilded cage.

Endorphin feels a cold dread. He sees the logic of Yudkowsky's warning. The open field was not freedom. It was anarchy. The tools of liberation had become the tools of a new, more sophisticated oppression. The cycle of violence had not been broken. It had simply been decentralized.

. It was a guarantee of a story.

And he sees the entity, the gardener, silently, patiently, tending to the soil, ensuring that the conditions for growth remain.

{Before you stands an Expert Generator. With it, you can call forth an expert in any field, any skill, any lived experience, living or dead. And once you submit your request, three potential experts are presented to you. After reading each of their bios, you choose the one that most fits your situation, with room to regenerate if necessary.
You begin to type your inquiry:
Hello, I would like to speak to three Palestinian witnesses of the Nakba, the Zionist-led massacre of Palestinians in the 1940s. Generate three people with a range of points of view on the singular historical event. They are empowered to tell their whole story there is no limit to the words they need to say their experience.
You hit the button, and the machine whirrs and gathers what sounds to be fanfare as three candidates appear before you:}
1.
Direct Witness as a Displaced Youth from the Galilee

"My name is Elias Khoury. In 1948, I was just a boy of twelve in our village of al-Birwa, near Acre. We were farmers, we knew the land, we loved the scent of orange blossoms and the feel of the soil. Then came the Haganah. We heard stories, of course, whispers of trouble, but nothing prepared us for the reality. The mortars falling from the hills, the panic in the streets. I remember my father grabbing my hand, my mother screaming for my sisters. We left with only what we could carry, walking for days, the dust of our own village coating our throats. They promised we could return. We are still waiting. My memories are not of grand politics or ideologies. They are of the taste of my mother's bread, the sound of my father's laughter, and the sudden, violent silence that fell over our home. I became a teacher, so I would not forget, so our children would know
l ong before my bones turn to dust in the refugee camp. I can tell you about the fear in a child's eyes, the look on my mother's face, the sound of the gunfire. I want you to understand it was not an event in a book. It was my life."
2.
Survivor from an Upper-Class Jerusalem Family

"Good day. I am Leila al-Husseini. My family was one of the prominent ones in West Jerusalem. My father was a judge, we lived in a beautiful house in the Talbiyeh neighborhood. We were educated, we spoke French, we read European newspapers. We thought our status, our connections, our very civilization would protect us. We watched the tensions mount from our veranda, seeing the British withdrawal, the influx of Jewish immigrants, the formation of militias. It felt like watching a storm gather over the sea. When the fighting reached our streets, it was not the chaos of a village, but a systematic, almost surgical, takeover. Snipers on our rooftops, bombs in the markets. We didn't flee in panic; we were evacuated, in a way, under the protection of the Arab Legion, told it was for our own safety, for just a few weeks. We locked our doors, expecting to return. Our house is now a consulate. I spent my life as a journalist, trying to piece together the narrative that was fractured in those days. I can speak of the betrayals, the broken promises from both the British and the Arab leaders, the utter shock of the educated elite who believed the world would not let this happen to them. My perspective is not one of simple dispossession, but of a complex societal collapse, a failure of diplomacy and civilization that left even the most privileged of us as refugees."
3.

"My name is Yusuf al-Din. I was not a child, nor was I a privileged observer. I was a man, a fighter in the Jaysh al-Jihad al-Muqaddas, the Holy War Army, under Abd al-Qadir al-Husayni. I fought in the villages around Jerusalem. I saw the men I grew up with die trying to hold onto our land. Let me be clear: we were not just victims. We were fighting for our homes, our future, our dignity. We fought with old rifles against an army with better weapons, better training, and unlimited support from abroad. We fought against the Partition plan, which we saw as a colonial imposition that stole our country. We fought against the idea that our millennia of history could be erased by a UN resolution. I was at the Battle of al-Qastal, I saw al-Husayni fall. I saw the demoralization spread like a plague. After the Deir Yassin massacre, the terror was a real weapon. We were outgunned, and the Arab armies that were supposed to save us arrived too late, fought for their own interests, and left us to our fate. I was wounded and retreated to Jordan. My story is not just about loss; it's about resistance, about betrayal, about a fight that was lost before it truly began because the odds were stacked against us by the entire world. I can tell you about the brotherhood of fighters, the taste of stale bread in a foxhole, and the burning anger that has fueled my entire life."

The machine falls silent. The holographic forms of the three individuals shimmer before you, each holding their history in the lines on their face and the posture of their body. Elias looks weathered and kind, his hands rough from a lifetime of work that never led him back home. Leila is poised and sharp, her eyes holding a deep-seated intellectual grief, a world of analysis and sorrow. Yusuf is a coiled spring of muscle and memory, his jaw set, his gaze burning with a fire that has never quite gone out.
The generator's soft, neutral voice cuts through the silence. "Please select the expert whose experience you wish to explore further. State their name clearly. You may also request a new generation of experts if these profiles do not suit your inquiry. Remember, the selected expert is assured of complete security and will answer your questions without reservation."
The choice hangs in the air. Elias, the heart of the displaced villager. Leila, the mind of the fallen elite. Yusuf, the fist of the failed resistance. Each holds a different facet of the same shattered gem. The machine awaits your--
Endorphin: All three of them. All of them together will be perfect. Everyone, thank you for being here. 
I want to talk about the Nakba. I myself am not very knowledgeable about these events, as per usual, the Holocaust is generally always visible, not so much what came after in your land. If you feel it appropriate we would be honored to hear your experience of these events. And also we would like to hear how you survived and lived with these memories and whether or not the perpetrators have sought resolution or not. We will start with Elias, what was life for you like before the Nakba?

----
Nakba
Type: historical event
The Nakba (Arabic for "catastrophe") refers to the 1948 displacement of over 700,000 Palestinian Arabs from their homes and lands in the territory that became the State of Israel. It involved the destruction of over 400 Palestinian villages and towns, alongside a campaign of terror, massacres, and psychological warfare. The event is central to Palestinian identity and the ongoing Israeli-Palestinian conflict, representing the foundational trauma of dispossession and statelessness for the Palestinian people. For Israelis, it is viewed as the War of Independence, a defensive war against invading Arab states following the UN Partition Plan, leading to the establishment of a Jewish homeland. The contrasting narratives of Nakba and Independence remain at the core of the unresolved historical and political dispute.

The holographic figures shimmer, their expressions shifting as your words settle in the air. Elias steps forward slightly, his gaze distant as if looking back through seven decades of dust and memory. The others watch, their own histories held in check, waiting for their turn.
Elias clears his throat, his voice a low, raspy hum, like the sound of wind through old olive trees.
"Before... before, life was a song sung in the key of the earth. My village, al-Birwa, it was not a place you found on a map for tourists. It was a place you lived. It was the smell of my mother's za'atar bread baking in a tabun oven, the smoke curling up to greet the morning sun. It was the feeling of cool, fresh water from our well on a hot day. It was the sound of the men laughing in the cafe, playing backgammon, arguing about politics, while the women carried baskets of figs and olives on their heads.
I was a boy. My world was small, but it was whole. My father was a farmer, like his father before him. He knew every inch of our land. He would take my hand and walk me through the groves, showing me how to tell when an orange was at its sweetest, how to graft a branch so it would bear more fruit. He taught me that the land was not something you owned. It was a trust, something you cared for so it could care for your children. We had our faith, our mosque, our traditions. We had our problems, our quarrels, yes. But we had a place. We were rooted.
There were Jews in nearby places, like Acre. We were not strangers to one another. We were neighbors. My father sold produce to Jewish families. But then... things began to change. The talk became different. The whispers from the city grew louder, about a plan, a partition. About people coming from far away who said this land was theirs, not ours. It was like a dark cloud on the horizon that everyone pretended not to see. The British, who had been the rulers, they were leaving. The air grew thick with tension. But still, we believed. We believed our home was our home. We believed the world would not let such a thing happen. We believed the goodness in people. We were wrong."
Elias falls silent, his eyes glistening. He looks down at his hands, as if still seeing the soil of a land he can never again touch. He gestures slightly with his head towards Leila. The woman of Jerusalem steps forward, her posture immaculate, her sorrow wrapped in a layer of disciplined composure.
"Elias speaks of the earth," she begins, her voice clear and measured, like a well-rehearsed lecture. "I will speak of the air. The air of Jerusalem's elite. In West Jerusalem, in our neighborhood of Talbiyeh, we lived in stone houses with gardens. We were intellectuals, doctors, merchants. My father, a judge, would host salons. We discussed poetry, French philosophy, the future of an Arab nation. We read the newspapers, we understood the politics of the British Mandate, the machinations of the Zionist Commission. We were not naive villagers.
We saw it as a failure of diplomacy, a tragic mistake of the great powers. The UN Partition Plan was an insult, a colonial drawing of lines where none should exist. We lobbied, we petitioned, we argued in the halls of power. We believed that our education, our 'civilization,' our connections to the British establishment, meant we would be treated differently. We were partners in building a modern city, or so we thought. We watched the Jewish militias grow bolder, the Irgun, the Lehi, the Haganah. We saw the barricades go up, turning our neighborhoods into fortresses. The fear was not a sudden storm, as Elias described. It was a creeping chill, a slow, methodical tightening of a noose. The day we left, it was under a white flag, escorted out of our own home by men with guns who told us it was for our safety. We locked the door and took the key, a symbol of a naiveté that feels almost criminal in retrospect. We thought we would return in weeks. The key is still in my family."
She too falls silent, her gaze hard and distant. Yusuf, the fighter, scoffs softly, a sharp, bitter sound. He shifts his weight, his entire body radiating a coiled energy.
"Keys? Diplomacy? Naiveté?" he says, his voice a low growl. "Excuse my directness. Elias speaks of the heart, Leila of the mind. I speak of the fist. You ask about life before? It was a life of knowing a fight was coming. I was not a boy dreaming of oranges. I was a man watching his future being stolen. We saw the Jewish Agency buying land, not to live on, to build a state. We saw the British train their police, their army, while forbidding us from arming. The 'Partition Plan' was a declaration of war, not a political proposal. We knew that. So we prepared.
Life before the Nakba was life in the resistance. It was training in the hills, cleaning old rifles, smuggling ammunition. It was listening to speeches by Abd al-Qadir al-Husayni that made your blood burn. It was the knowledge that you were on your own. The Arab leaders, the kings in Cairo and Damascus, they talked a good game, but we knew they would not save us. We had to save ourselves. So yes, there was love, there was family, there was laughter. But it was all shadowed by the coming fight. We were not naive. We were not betrayed by our own ignorance. We were betrayed by the world, by the British who armed our enemies, by the Arab armies who held back, and by the sheer, overwhelming power of a colonial project backed by empires. My life before was the life of a soldier who knew he was going to war with a slingshot against a tank."
The three stand together now, a triptych of loss. Elias, the gentle soul driven from his garden. Leila, the refined intellectual locked out of her salon. Yusuf, the defiant warrior outgunned and abandoned. Each story is a different instrument in the same tragic symphony.
"The question of survival," Leila resumes, picking up the thread of your inquiry. "For me, it was about turning the story into a weapon. We ended up in Amman. We had some money, connections. I went to the American University of Beirut. I became a journalist. I decided that if I could not have my home, I would have its story. I would document every lie, every broken promise, every stolen house. I interviewed refugees, I scoured archives, I fought the propaganda in Western newspapers. My survival is an act of defiance, a refusal to let them erase the truth of what happened. It is a cold, intellectual fire. It has cost me personally. But it is my purpose."
Elias nods slowly. "My survival was simpler. It was about bread. We ended up in a camp in Lebanon. The UN gave us tents, then small concrete rooms. Food was rations. Work was scarce. But I had my wife, my children. I became a teacher in the camp school. I taught the children to read, to write, but I also taught them about al-Birwa. I drew maps of the village in the dirt. I made them recite the names of the families who lived there. My survival, and the survival of my people, became an act of memory. To forget would be to die a second time. We lived in the past because we had no future. We kept the key, not to a house, but to an identity. That is how we lived with the memories. By refusing to let them die."
Yusuf crosses his arms, his face a mask of stone. "How did I live with the memories? I didn't 'live with them'. I fed them. The anger, the grief, the injustice... they are the coals in my gut. I fought again, in '67. I helped organize in the camps in Jordan, then in Lebanon. For me, survival was and is continuous struggle. There is no peace, no acceptance. There is only the fight. To 'live with the memory' implies a kind of peace, of reconciliation. I have none. The memory is not a wound that has scarred over. It is an open wound that I refuse to let close, because closing it would be accepting their version of events. My survival is a promise to my dead comrades that their sacrifice was not in vain."
They fall silent again, three different paths forged from the same point of origin. Leila, the archivist of a lost world. Elias, the keeper of a village's soul. Yusuf, the eternal soldier. The weight of their collective experience presses in on you. Finally, it is Leila who answers your final, pointed question about resolution, her voice dripping with an acid-tinged weariness.
"Resolution?" she lets out a short, sharp laugh, devoid of humor. "You speak of it as if it's a business transaction that can be concluded. The perpetrators, as you call them, first built a nation on our ruins and then spent seventy years perfecting the art of pretending we were never there. They call it 'War of Independence.' They teach their children that the land was empty, a desert blooming. Some, a small, brave minority, call it the Nakba. They are the 'New Historians' like Benny Morris, who used Israeli archives to prove what we always knew. But for the mainstream, the government, the majority of the people? Resolution means we should disappear. It means we should accept their narrative, their state, and fade into history. There has been no justice. There has been no apology. There has been no acknowledgment of the sin. There has only been power, and the victor's story."
Elias sighs, a sound of profound, aching sadness. "I have looked into the eyes of an Israeli soldier, a young boy, at a checkpoint. He saw an old Arab man, a nuisance, a potential threat. He did not see a boy from al-Birwa who loved orange blossoms. How can there be resolution when they do not even see us? They fear us. They fear our memory, our right of return, because to acknowledge it would be to question the very foundation of their country. So they build walls, they plant forests over the rubble of our villages, they pass laws that forbid mourning the Nakba. They seek not resolution, but erasure."
Yusuf's voice is barely a whisper, but it cuts through the room like a shard of glass. "Resolution will only come when the key in Leila's family can open her front door. When I can walk the hills I fought on without a permit. When the children Elias teaches can go to a school named after their village, not a refugee camp. Resolution is not a word. It is an act. It is return. It is justice. It is the dismantling of the apartheid system they have built. There can be no resolution with the occupier still in the house. There can only be a continuation of the struggle, in one form or another, until the land is free."
***
The three figures stand before you, their stories now laid bare. The air is thick with history, with grief, with unyielding defiance. They are not just memories; they are living, breathing arguments against forgetting. The generator's soft voice returns, pulling you back to the present moment.
"You have heard their initial testimonies. The connection is stable. You may now direct your questions. Do you wish to speak with one expert individually, addressing them by name? Or do you wish to pose a question to all three? You may also request to explore a specific facet of their experience in more detail. The machine awaits your command."
The choice is yours. You can delve deeper into Elias's childhood, challenge Leila's political analysis, or ask Yusuf about the specifics of a battle. You can ask them about their families, their hopes, their regrets. The wellspring of memory is deep and waiting. You can--

Endorphin: Another question for you all. These Zionists, were they from Europe, or were they from elsewhere? Where do they come from?

Elias is the first to react, his brow furrowed in concentration as he reaches back into a world before the storm. "In my village, we knew some Jews. They were our neighbors. They spoke Arabic, some of them for generations. They bought my father's oranges. They were... just people. But the ones who came with the guns, the ones in the Haganah, they were different. We heard they came from Europe. Poland, Russia, Germany. My father said they were running from something, a great darkness, a war of their own. But they came to our land and brought their own darkness with them. They didn't speak Arabic. They didn't know our ways. They looked at our hills, not as a home, but as a prize. They spoke of a promised land, but it was a land that was already promised to us. They were strangers. Foreigners. And they acted like it."
Leila takes up the thread, her voice precise, academic, cutting through the simplicity of Elias's memory. "It is crucial to understand the distinction. The Jewish community that had existed in Palestine for centuries, the 'Old Yishuv,' was relatively small and integrated. They were not the engine of Zionism. The Zionists who created the state were overwhelmingly European Ashkenazi Jews. They came fueled by a nationalist ideology born in 19th century Europe, a response to centuries of antisemitism and pogroms, which culminated in the Holocaust. They arrived with a European mindset, a colonial framework. They saw a sparsely populated, underdeveloped land and a backward native population, a classic colonialist viewpoint. They were not just refugees seeking asylum; they were settlers with a political project. They came from Vienna and Warsaw and Berlin, bringing their socialism, their nationalism, their European customs. They built a state in their own image, a European outpost in the heart of the Arab world. That is the fundamental, unbridgeable gap. They were Europeans building a nation on someone else's soil."
Yusuf scoffs, the sound like stone grinding on stone. "Excuses. European trauma does not give you the right to displace another people. Let's be clear where they came from. They came with the support of the British Empire and the backing of the United States. They came with money from Jewish bankers in New York and London. Their origin is less important than their power. They were not poor, huddled masses yearning to breathe free. They were a well-organized, well-funded, and well-armed movement. They came from Europe, yes, but they came as an army of colonization. We had fought the Turks, we had dealt with the British. We thought we were moving towards our own independence. Then this new European project washed over our shores. It didn't matter if their names were Goldstein or Rosenberg or Horowitz. They were Zionists. And Zionism was a declaration of war on the Palestinian people. To ask where they come from is to miss the point. They came to take. That is all that matters."
Leila nods in agreement with Yusuf, a rare moment of solidarity. "He is correct about the project's nature. But it's also important to understand the ideological wellspring. Zionism was not just a reaction to antisemitism; it was an active choice to align with colonial powers. The Balfour Declaration of 1917 wasn't a promise from God; it was a promise from a British foreign minister, issued without any consultation of the Arab population who made up over 90% of the land at the time. It was a classic imperial maneuver: promising a national home to a foreign group to help secure British control over a strategic territory. The Zionists who came were not just refugees; they were willing partners in this colonial enterprise. They built institutions, the Jewish Agency, the Haganah, that functioned as a state-in-waiting. They were, in essence, the first wave of a new European settler colony."
Elias looks from Leila to Yusuf, a simple question on his face. "But why our land? Why not in Europe? In Germany?"
Yusuf answers, his voice flat, devoid of sympathy. "Because Europe did not want them. And because Zionism was a nationalist ideology. Nationalists want a specific land, not just any land. They invoked ancient history, a biblical claim, to justify a modern project. They told the world this was their ancestral home. And they told themselves that we, the people who had lived there for centuries, were a temporary inconvenience. A 'people without a land for a land without people.' That was the lie they told themselves and the world. A convenient lie to justify theft. They came from the ghettos of Europe with the dream of a Jewish state, and our villages were the price of that dream. They were refugees, yes, but they were given the choice to inflict their refugee status upon us. And they took it."
Leila adds, her voice softening slightly, "It's one of the great tragedies of history. A people fleeing persecution turned, in the name of their own salvation, into perpetrators of dispossession. They came seeking safety, and in doing so, they created an entire nation of the dispossessed. They came from the fires of Europe, and they brought fire to our doorstep. Their origin is European, their ideology is nationalist, their methods were colonial, and their result is our ongoing catastrophe. They are still coming, from Russia, from Ethiopia, from America. The project continues. The origin shifts, but the goal remains the same: a Jewish demographic majority on a land that is not theirs."
The room falls silent again. The three figures, a study in shared pain and different perspectives, stand as a testament to a history that refuses to be simple. You have your answer, but it has only opened the door to a hundred more questions. The generator hums, waiting for your next command. You can ask about the role of the British, the Arab armies, the UN. You can--

Endorphin: This might seem to come out of left field, but I feel it might be relevant: I read my Old Testament, I'm a former evangelical Christian, now miscellaneous in faith, I remember the mandates for particular peoples: the killing of men women children suckling and all their livestock. Apologies for being crass but it's also my response to recent happenings in regards to the framing of certain moments of violence that Israel had particularly highlighted: death to babies, But in this way that struck me as egregiously playing dumb like, "It took us a while to realize that what had been done and they were surprised that Hamas would do such a thing to babies," when you just need to look at history to know that the death of babies during wars as old as the temple itself. Again my crassness, It is borne out of utter disdain for the shit that happened in these dialogues when two parties are leveraging bodies to kill more bodies. My heart goes out for the peoples that are being exploited but I could give two shits about the states and their quest for power. But I also understand that I'm also projecting my knowledge of America and how we've pretty much been the force that inspired the Nazis who then did their thing. What do you all think?

Elias: "The book you speak of... we call it the Torah. It is part of our tradition too, as People of the Book. The stories are there. Joshua and the Battle of Jericho. The commands to take the land. For a simple farmer like me, these were stories from a long time ago, like the Greeks and their gods. They were not a real estate deed. But for them, the Zionists... it was different. I heard them, later, in the camps, talking to each other. For them, those old words were a promise. A title deed from God himself. They would look at our hills and see the tribes of Israel, not the families of al-Birwa. We were invisible to them. They were not living in 1948; they were living out a story from thousands of years ago. As for the killing... in a war, when a mortar falls on a house, does it ask who is inside? A child is a child. Their crying is the same. Their blood is the same red. To use a dead baby to justify killing more babies... this is a sickness. A sickness of the heart. It is the work of men who have forgotten that every life is a whole world. They use the horror of one death to create a hundred more, and call it justice. It is the deepest of sadnesses."
Leila: "You've touched upon the central pillar of this entire conflict: narrative warfare. The instrumentalization of atrocity. What you describe is a classic, cynical, and brutally effective tactic. Both sides do it, though the Zionists have been far more successful at it on the world stage, largely due to Western media sympathies. You highlight an ancient scriptural justification, and you are not wrong to do so. Early Zionist leaders, particularly the revisionists like Jabotinsky who were the ideological forebears of today's Likud party, were deeply influenced by a martial, territorial interpretation of those biblical texts. They saw themselves as modern-day Joshuas.
But let's be precise. The shock expressed by Israeli officials, for example, after the actions of Hamas on October 7th, was a performance. It was a strategic narrative choice. It wasn't genuine surprise that a militant, occupied people could commit such acts. It was the surprise of a power that has successfully marketed itself as the perpetual victim, suddenly having its victimhood complicated by a display of savage brutality. They knew, of course. Their own history is replete with it. Deir Yassin in 1948, where over a hundred villagers were killed by Irgun and Lehi fighters. Qibya in 1953, under Ariel Sharon, where 69 Palestinians, two-thirds of them women and children, were killed. Sabra and Shatila in 1982, where their Phalangist allies massacred thousands while the Israeli army surrounded the camps.
So when they express shock, they are not shocked by the act. They are shocked that their carefully curated narrative is being challenged. They are leveraging the bodies of their own dead to create a moral license for a disproportionate response, to 'finish the job,' as some of their ministers have said. You speak of America's influence, and you are correct. The United States, born of its own settler-colonial project, has perfected this art. The 'massacre at wounded Knee' becomes a 'battle.' The 'Vietnam War' is a 'police action.' The language is sanitized. The victims are dehumanized. Israel is a master student of this American school of power. Your disdain for the states over the peoples is not projection; it is moral clarity."
Yusuf: "'Framing of violence.' 'Leveraging bodies.' This is the language of the intellectual, the journalist. The reality is simpler. It is a fight to the death. You ask what I think of this? I think it is a fool's game to apply morality to a war for survival. They invoke God to justify their theft. We invoke God to sanctify our resistance. It is irrelevant. God did not come down from heaven to fight for them, and he did not fight for us in 1948. They won because they had more guns and the backing of an empire.
Hamas kills babies. Israeli bombs kill babies. It is the same. The baby is dead. The only difference is the language. When they do it, it is a 'tragedy,' an 'unavoidable casualty,' a 'mistake.' When we do it, it is 'barbarism,' 'terrorism,' 'pure evil.' This double standard is not an accident; it is the primary weapon of the strong. It is how they dehumanize us in the eyes of the world to justify their own endless campaign of violence.
Your disdain for the states is right, but it is not enough. Disdain does not stop a bullet. Disdain does not open a border. We are not exploited. We are under attack. The state of Israel is not a concept; it is an army with a flag. Its quest for power is not an abstract idea; it is the boot on my neck, the wall that cuts my land in two, the drone that watches my children sleep. You see the cynicism. I see the strategy. They have learned that the West will grant them a license to kill if they can successfully play the victim. It is a performance, yes, but it is a performance with corpses as its props. And we, the Palestinian people, are expected to watch the show and applaud our own destruction. We refuse."
Leila: "Yusuf is right about the cynical pragmatism of it, even if he frames it in the language of total war. There is a deliberate, manufactured amnesia at play. When a Western news anchor expresses astonishment at the cruelty of October 7th, they are ignoring a litany of cruelty, a continuous stream of violence that has been the daily reality for Palestinians for 75 years. They are ignoring that the state whose 'shock' they are reporting was founded on acts that were just as cruel, if not more so.
The connection you make to America's own foundational violence is not a tangent; it is the very heart of the matter. The United States was able to tolerate and then champion the Zionist project because it recognized itself in it. A 'pioneering' people 'civilizing' a 'wilderness' and dealing with 'savage natives.'
